chief_complaint: progressive difficulty climbing stairs or lifting arms with purple rash on knuckles and eyelids
hpi_details: 44F presenting with several weeks of progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs and lifting her arms overhead) with a violaceous rash around her eyes and over her knuckles.
ideas: She thinks she is suffering from severe physical exhaustion from overwork combined with an allergic reaction to a new skin cream.
concerns: She is worried that she is becoming paralyzed and will soon lose her independence and be unable to climb the stairs or dress herself.
expectations: She hopes to receive a prescription rash cream and blood tests to check for vitamin deficiencies or thyroid trouble that could explain her weakness.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Dermatomyositis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes confirmatory serology/EMG plus mandatory screening for interstitial lung disease and occult malignancy before or alongside immunosuppressive therapy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive difficulty climbing stairs or lifting arms with purple rash on knuckles and eyelids

Key HPI features: 44F presenting with several weeks of progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs and lifting her arms overhead) with a violaceous rash around her eyes and over her knuckles.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Symmetric proximal muscle weakness (hip and shoulder girdles), difficulty rising from a chair without arm support. Heliotrope rash on the upper eyelids with periorbital edema. Gottron's papules over the MCP/PIP joints and dorsal hands. Lung auscultation for fine crackles suggesting interstitial lung disease. No lymphadenopathy or palpable masses on exam today.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Dermatomyositis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Polymyositis (no rash) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Difficulty swallowing or breathing — suggests involvement of the pharyngeal or respiratory muscles.
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis with muscle enzymes (CK, aldolase), myositis-specific/associated antibodies (including anti-Jo-1), EMG, and muscle biopsy if the diagnosis remains uncertain
Screen for interstitial lung disease with HRCT chest and pulmonary function tests, particularly if antisynthetase antibodies (e.g., anti-Jo-1) are present
Perform age- and sex-appropriate malignancy screening given the strong dermatomyositis-cancer association in adults, and repeat periodically after diagnosis

Initiate immunosuppressive therapy (corticosteroids plus a steroid-sparing agent) under rheumatology direction, and screen for dysphagia/aspiration risk and respiratory muscle involvement requiring urgent escalation.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 44F presenting with several weeks of progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs and lifting her arms overhead) with a violaceous rash around her eyes and over her knuckles.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Symmetric proximal muscle weakness (hip and shoulder girdles), difficulty rising from a chair without arm support. Heliotrope rash on the upper eyelids with periorbital edema. Gottron's papules over the MCP/PIP joints and dorsal hands. Lung auscultation for fine crackles. No lymphadenopathy or palpable masses.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation (symmetric proximal weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules) highly suggestive of dermatomyositis; confirmatory CK and myositis-specific antibody testing pending.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm with CK/muscle enzymes, myositis-specific antibody panel (including anti-Jo-1), EMG, and muscle biopsy if uncertain. Screen for interstitial lung disease with HRCT chest and PFTs, and perform age- and sex-appropriate malignancy screening given the strong dermatomyositis-cancer association. Refer to rheumatology for immunosuppressive therapy and screen for dysphagia/aspiration and respiratory muscle involvement.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Dermatomyositis Proximal Myopathy
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for progressive difficulty climbing stairs or lifting arms with purple rash on knuckles and eyelids
Select appropriate confirmatory testing (myositis antibodies, EMG) and screening (HRCT for ILD, age-appropriate malignancy screening) for newly diagnosed dermatomyositis
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing symmetric proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs, raising arms) along with characteristic skin findings — a heliotrope rash around the eyes and Gottron's papules on the knuckles.
red_flags: Difficulty swallowing or breathing — suggests involvement of the pharyngeal or respiratory muscles

must_ask.say: Which is harder — climbing stairs or lifting your arms above your head?
Where is the purple rash — around your eyes and on your knuckles?
How long has the weakness been developing?
Does the rash get worse in the sun?
Have you had any unexplained weight loss, new lumps, or changes in bowel habits or bleeding?

history.answer: I have had so much weakness in my arms and legs for the past several weeks, and it has gotten so bad that I can barely climb stairs or lift my arms up to wash my hair.
It is genuine loss of muscle strength rather than numbness or tingling, and my limbs just feel heavy and fatigued.
It affects both of my upper arms and thighs equally on both sides, while my hands and feet still seem pretty normal.
It started gradually about six weeks ago and has steadily gotten worse week by week.
I have to push off with my arms to stand up from a low chair and cannot reach overhead cupboards, but I can still button clothes and hold pens without trouble.
The weakness stays about the same throughout the entire day and does not feel significantly worse in the late afternoon or evening.
No, I do not have any neck pain, lower back pain, or radiating pain shooting down my arms or legs.
No, my face does not droop, my speech is completely clear, and I have not had any dizziness or vision changes.
I have not had any shortness of breath or chest tightness, and I can swallow food and drinks without choking.
No, I have not had droopy eyelids or seen double at any time.
My bladder control and bowel movements are completely normal, and I have no numbness around my groin or buttocks.
I have not seen any twitching under the skin or shrinking of my muscles.
No, I did not have a cold, fever, cough, or diarrhea before this weakness began.
Around the time the weakness started, I noticed a purplish-red rash on my upper eyelids and over the knuckles of both hands.
Yes, whenever I am out in the bright sun, the rash on my skin tends to look redder and feel more irritated.
I have been feeling exhausted, but I have not had any fevers, night sweats, or unexpected weight loss.
No, I have never had high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, stroke, or heart rhythm problems.
I eat regular meals including meat and vegetables, and I have never had stomach surgery or followed a strict vegan diet.
I work at a desk and do not perform heavy repetitive wrist motions, lean heavily on my elbows, or squat for hours.
I figured the rash was just an allergic reaction to a new face cream and my weak muscles were from burning out at work.
I'm terrified that my legs will give out on the stairs and that I won't even be able to lift my arms to brush my own hair or get dressed.
I hope you can give me an ointment for this rash around my eyes and run some blood tests to see if a severe vitamin deficiency is making me so weak.
I have always been healthy and do not have any chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries or stayed in the hospital overnight.
I do not take any prescription drugs, cholesterol-lowering statins, steroids, or over-the-counter supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I drink one or two glasses of wine socially on weekends, nothing heavy.
I work full-time as an office manager and live at home with my husband and two children.
Nobody in my family has had muscle diseases, autoimmune disorders, or young-onset cancers.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, my periods are regular every four weeks, my husband and I use condoms, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 72/min regular, respiratory rate 14/min, temperature 36.7°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Violaceous erythema with mild periorbital edema on both upper eyelids, and violaceous erythematous papules over the dorsal MCP and PIP joints bilaterally.

Symmetric proximal muscle weakness with deltoids and hip flexors graded 4-/5 bilaterally, while distal muscle strength including grip and ankle dorsiflexion is preserved at 5/5; no muscle atrophy or fasciculations.
Difficulty rising from a seated position without using arm support; waddling gait pattern noted, but coordination and tandem walk are preserved.
Light touch, pinprick, and vibration sensation are completely normal and symmetric across all four limbs without stocking-glove sensory loss.
Biceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally; plantar responses are flexor with no Babinski sign.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact, with symmetric facial movements, no ptosis, normal extraocular movements, and normal soft palate elevation.
Fine end-inspiratory crackles audible over both lung bases posteriorly; no wheezing or rhonchi.
No palpable lymphadenopathy in the cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary regions.
No cervical or lumbar vertebral tenderness; bilateral straight-leg raise tests are negative.
